name: Musée Mohammed VI d'Art Moderne et Contemporain (MMVI)
funding: State museum run since 2014 by the Fondation Nationale des Musées, built with Ministry of Culture and Fonds Hassan II money.
watch: Morocco's first national museum of modern and contemporary art, opened October 2014 by the king; FNM president Mehdi Qotbi.
tier_note: No reason for the flag is recorded.
affiliations_note: Run by the Fondation Nationale des Musées, which lists it among 22 museums across Morocco, including the Musée National de la Photographie in Rabat.

overview: State museum of modern and contemporary art at 2 Avenue Moulay Hassan in Rabat, described as the first museum in Morocco devoted entirely to modern and contemporary art (Fondation Nationale des Musées).
Founded on the initiative of King Mohammed VI. It opened in October 2014 with the exhibition "1914 to 2014: 100 Years of Creation" (Wikipedia, Yabiladi).

Building: 6,813 m2 over three floors at the corner of avenues Moulay El Hassan and Allal Ben Abdellah, designed by architect Karim Chakor, who drew on the monumental administrative buildings of the French protectorate (Bladi, Fouad Boumnadel, 22 July 2014).
The museum is run by the Fondation Nationale des Musées (FNM). Le360 (2018) names Mehdi Qotbi as head of the FNM and Abdelaziz Idrissi as the museum's director.

The collection holds more than 500 paintings and about ten sculptures, built by purchase, donation and long-term loan (FNM). The museum hosts yearly international temporary exhibitions, with past shows on Picasso, Giacometti, Goya and Delacroix (FNM).
Visiting: open 10:00 to 18:00, closed Tuesdays. Admission is 30 DH for Moroccan adults, 15 DH for Moroccans under 18 and 60 DH for foreign visitors (FNM).
details.funding_verdict: Musée Mohammed VI d'Art Moderne et Contemporain: building paid by the Fonds Hassan II and the Ministry of Culture
funding: Construction cost more than 200 million dirhams, financed by the Fonds Hassan II pour le développement économique et social; the Ministry of Culture, as project owner, contributed 44 million dirhams (Bladi, Fouad Boumnadel, "Ouverture du musée national d'art contemporain à Rabat", 22 July 2014).
The museum is run by the Fondation Nationale des Musées, which operates fourteen museums of the national network (FNM, Wikipedia).

red_flags.heading: State censorship allegation at the 2014 opening
points: Unverified: artist Mounir Fatmi, in a Facebook post reported by Yabiladi (Ghita Ismaili, 21 October 2014), said his installation "Face au Silence", a homage to Mehdi Ben Barka, was not shown at the opening of "100 ans de création" on 7 October 2014. Citing visitors, he said the museum management excluded political works and works about the body or nudity.

The museum told Yabiladi the work was never censored, had been on display since the public opening on 9 October 2014, with photo evidence, and that the video could not be projected on inauguration day because of a technical problem fixed the next day.

press.overall: Little criticism in art media. Moroccan press covered a censorship complaint in 2014 and criticised the programming in 2018.

items.title: Qods Chabaa, "Polémique autour d'une exposition bâclée au musée Mohammed VI" (16 October 2018)
points: Reports that Hossein Talal, son of painter Chaïbia Talal, was told the show would be a solo tribute to his mother and learned of the group format from the press.
The piece questions the show's scientific basis and accuses Mehdi Qotbi, head of the FNM, of prioritising costly international exhibitions over support for Moroccan artists.
Museum director Abdelaziz Idrissi answered that several people were consulted, no contract was signed, and the group format placed Chaïbia's work in the context of the 1960s.

items.title: Ghita Ismaili, "Une oeuvre de Mounir Fatmi censurée ? Le Musée Mohammed VI de Rabat réfute" (21 October 2014)
points: Reports Fatmi's complaint and the museum's denial, without verifying either side.

details.bottom_line: The building was paid for by the Fonds Hassan II (more than 200 million dirhams) and the Ministry of Culture (44 million dirhams), and the FNM runs the museum. The one documented dispute is Mounir Fatmi's 2014 censorship claim, which the museum denied.

name: Heroes' Acre (Windhoek)
funding: Namibian government paid Mansudae N$60 million against a N$34 million budget. Opened 26 August 2002. The National Heritage Council runs it; adult Namibians paid N$50 in 2024-25.
watch: Insight Namibia's corruption tracker (March 2008) says the contract cost twice the first estimate. UN Panel report S/2017/150 lists the site among Mansudae's Namibian works.
why_flagged: Insight Namibia's corruption tracker (March 2008) says the contract cost twice the first estimate. UN Panel report S/2017/150 lists the site among Mansudae's Namibian works.
records_note: The National Heritage Council gazettes the admission fees (Government Gazette No. 8206, September 2023).
finances_note: Admission fees raised N$64,188 in 2006 against upkeep of N$500,000 a year (Van der Hoog, Leiden University thesis, 2024, p.147, citing The Namibian, 2002 to 2006).
affiliations_note: Run by the National Heritage Council of Namibia, the statutory body under the National Heritage Act 2004 that sets admission fees for protected places.

propaganda.summary: Namibia's government commissioned the national memorial from North Korea's Mansudae Overseas Projects; it opened in August 2002. A 2017 Leiden study states the site legitimizes the rule of the former liberation movement SWAPO.

overview: National war memorial and burial ground in the hills about 10 kilometres south of Windhoek's centre, on the B1 road to Rehoboth. It opened on 26 August 2002 (Wikipedia).

Founding president Sam Nujoma started the project (Wikipedia). Mansudae Overseas Projects designed and built it, and Van der Hoog calls it, like Zimbabwe's Acre, a copy of the Revolutionary Martyrs' Cemetery near Pyongyang.
A marble obelisk, a bronze Unknown Soldier, parade grounds with a grandstand for 5,000 and 174 tombs (Wikipedia).
Presidents Hage Geingob and Sam Nujoma are buried there (Wikipedia).

Visiting: for 1 April 2024 to 30 April 2025 the National Heritage Council set admission at N$50 for Namibian adults self-guided and N$60 guided, N$70 and N$80 for international adults, with young children free (Government Gazette No. 8206).
details.funding_verdict: Heroes' Acre (Windhoek): public: Government of Namibia paid for the build; the National Heritage Council runs it
funding: The Acre was budgeted at N$34 million and realised for N$60 million (Van der Hoog, Leiden University thesis, 2024, p.147).

The National Heritage Council, the statutory body under the National Heritage Act 2004, sets the fees (Government Gazette No. 8206, 4 September 2023) and administers the site (Navigate Namibia). The Ministry of Works and Transport has the mandate of keeping it up to standard (New Era, 4 July 2017).

red_flags.heading: Contract cost and tendering
points: Insight Namibia's Corruption Tracker (March 2008) said Mansudae's Heroes' Acre contract ended up costing twice the first expectation, and that Mansudae's State House contract went out with no competitive tender.

The final cost of N$60 million against a N$34 million budget is recorded by Van der Hoog (p.147), who adds that African governments usually award Mansudae projects by closed tender, so total payments cannot be determined (p.148).

red_flags.heading: Contractor named in UN Panel reports
points: S/2017/150, table 4, lists the Hero's Acre among Mansudae's works in Namibia. Para 118 gives the Panel's grounds for recommending Mansudae's designation: services related to arms, the Oamites munitions factory built on behalf of KOMID, and bulk cash transfers by its workers.

Namibia announced in June 2016 that it would end the services of KOMID and Mansudae (para 112). On 17 November 2017 it told the Panel that all North Korean workers had left, and supplied cancellation orders for two Mansudae projects dated 9 August 2017 and documents on a third (S/2018/171, paras 104 to 106).

Mansudae Overseas Project Group of Companies was blocked by the US on 2 December 2016 and listed by the UN and EU with a designation date of 5 August 2017. Van der Hoog notes the 2006 sanctions regime did not criminalise construction work (p.148).

not_related: the National Heroes' Acre near Harare, Zimbabwe, is a separate site built by the same contractor in 1981 to 1982 and run by Zimbabwe's Department of Museums and National Monuments.

press.overall: Criticism concerns money and contracting, not the design. Two pieces were opened.

items.title: Corruption Tracker, "The hidden world of public contracting" (March 2008)
points: Names the Heroes' Acre contract as costing twice the first estimate and the State House award to Mansudae as untendered.
Criticises procurement, not the monument's design.

items.title: Tycho van der Hoog, "North Korea and the Liberation of Southern Africa, 1960-2020", chapter 15, "Money: Nationalism as a Business Model" (2024)
points: Says North Korean projects tend to cost much more than planned, and gives the Acre's budget, cost and upkeep.
Criticises the contracting, not the design.

details.bottom_line: Namibian public money paid for the Acre, and no flagged funder was found. The weak points are the overrun from a N$34 million budget to a N$60 million cost, the 2008 watchdog's complaint about the same contractor's untendered State House award, and Mansudae's 2017 UN and EU listing, after a Panel report that cited its munitions-factory work elsewhere in Namibia. Worth watching: the upkeep burden on the National Heritage Council.

name: National Art Gallery of Namibia
funding: State-owned art gallery. Bank Windhoek partners on its 2025/2026 Triennial.
watch: In March 2014 the gallery asked artist Paolo Solari Bozzi to withdraw photos of Himba girls; he pulled the whole show. The gallery denied censorship.
why_flagged: In March 2014 the gallery asked artist Paolo Solari Bozzi to withdraw photos of Himba girls; he pulled the whole show. The gallery denied censorship.
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.
records_note: NAGN posts annual reports for 2019/20 to 2024/25 with audited statements, names its seven trustees, and names its strategic partners in the latest report.
finances_note: FY2024-25 income NAD 9.81M: about 90 percent Ministry of Education, Arts and Culture, 7 percent earned, 2 percent foundation and donor money (audited statements p. 56).

overview: State-owned art gallery in central Windhoek, at the corner of Robert Mugabe Avenue and John Meinert Street (NAGN site).
Founded in 1990 (Wikipedia). Its site calls it "Namibia's premier institution for the collection, preservation, and promotion of visual arts and crafts" (stated by the gallery).
Permanent exhibition of Namibian, African and European art, plus exhibitions by local artists (Wikipedia).

Hosts the Bank Windhoek Triennial, "Namibia's biggest visual art competition" (NAGN's words). The 2025/2026 theme is "Namibian Identity: The Linework of a Country's Contours and Wealth", with a N$50,000 first prize and a solo exhibition at the gallery, a launch on 6 August 2026 and a submission deadline of 27 May 2026 (NAGN triennial page).
Leadership: Wikipedia lists Michelle Olga van Wyk as CEO, Snobia Kaputu as CEO from 2017 to 2022 and Hercules Viljoen as director from 2012 to 2017.
Visiting: Monday 14:00 to 17:00, Tuesday to Friday 08:00 to 17:00, Saturday 09:00 to 14:00, closed Sunday.
details.funding_verdict: National Art Gallery of Namibia: public: a state-owned gallery, with Bank Windhoek as partner of its triennial
funding: State-owned (NAGN site, Wikipedia).

Bank Windhoek hosts the 2025/2026 Triennial in partnership with the gallery; the page states prizes of N$50,000, N$35,000 and N$25,000 but not who pays them or the bank's amount (NAGN triennial page).

red_flags.heading: 2014 exhibition withdrawn over photographs of Himba girls
points: March 2014: the gallery objected to photographs of what the excerpts call underage girls in Paolo Solari Bozzi's show based on his book "Namibia Sun Pictures", which was set to open on 3 March 2014. The gallery contended the girls were too young to consent to being photographed and tried to negotiate with him to withdraw those photographs; he withdrew the whole series instead. This account rests on search-result excerpts of ARTICLE 19 and the Censorpedia wiki of the National Coalition Against Censorship; both pages returned 403 when opened, and no news report of the episode was found.

The excerpts say the gallery denied that this was censorship, saying the decision to withdraw the whole series was the artist's (stated by the gallery), and that critics noted the arbitrary nature of its request. Both statements come from the same excerpts.

press.overall: The 2014 episode is recorded by free-expression groups, not by art press.

details.bottom_line: The gallery's money is Namibian state funding with Bank Windhoek attached to the triennial; no funder with a documented controversy was found. The weak points are the 2014 withdrawal of a photography show, which the gallery says was the artist's choice and which is documented only in excerpts of two free-expression group pages, and the lack of readable income figures. Worth watching: the amount of the state grant and Bank Windhoek's share in the annual reports.

name: Kijk-Kubus
funding: Not confirmed. The Het Blaakse Bos Foundation runs the show cube and charges EUR 3.50 admission.
watch: Furnished show cube in Piet Blom's 1984 Cube Houses, which are mostly private homes. Site names founder Ed R. de Graaf.
records_note: Publishes opening hours, ticket prices and contact details only.
affiliations_note: Operated by the Het Blaakse Bos Foundation, as the museum's own contact page states. Listed in the Iconic Houses network.

overview: Furnished show cube in the Cube Houses at Overblaak 70, Rotterdam, in the east of the city centre near Blaak station, the Market Hall, the library and the Old Harbour (museum site).

Piet Blom designed the Cube Houses, built from 1982 to 1984 after plans were first shown in 1978: 38 cube houses and 13 business cubes (Dutch Wikipedia). The museum site names Ed R. de Graaf as founder of the show cube and says it "opens its door this year for the 42nd season", with no year given.
Kijk-Kubus is the museum's name. The complex is nicknamed the Blaakse Bos, the Blaak Forest, because each cube stands for a tree (museum site, Dutch Wikipedia).
Each cube sits on one pole and has three levels, with a kitchen and living room on the lowest. The complex stands above the Overblaak viaduct and is a municipal monument (Dutch Wikipedia).

On site: a cube decorated with slanted walls and custom-built furniture, screens, info panels and a model of the architecture (museum site). The Kunstkubus at Overblaak 30 and a chess piece museum at Overblaak 94 are separate (Dutch Wikipedia).

Visiting: the home page says open daily 10:00 to 18:00, to 19:00 in July and August. The visit page lists 10:00 to 18:00 and 11:00 to 17:00. Tickets EUR 3.50, EUR 2.50 for ages 65 and over and students, EUR 1.50 up to age 12, free up to age 4. Rotterdampas holders free. Three floors with steep stairs. No formal accessibility information (museum site).
details.funding_verdict: Kijk-Kubus: not confirmed: ticket income at EUR 3.50 for a foundation that publishes no accounts
funding: The visit page says the Het Blaakse Bos Foundation runs the show cube; the home page names no operator and credits only its web maker.
The surrounding Cube Houses are privately owned homes (Dutch Wikipedia).
details.bottom_line: The only visible money is ticket income, and no funder or owner is named. The weak points are the missing accounts, the missing ANBI number and board names, and a visit page that still announces a COVID closure. Worth watching: whether the foundation ever publishes accounts or names an owner.

name: TENT Rotterdam
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.

overview: Contemporary art space at Coolhaven 32, Rotterdam, presenting Rotterdam artists and projects through a fixed location and nomadic projects. It describes itself as a programme of CBK Rotterdam (stated by the space).

Grew out of a Rotterdam exhibition platform that became TENT from 1999, later at Witte de Withstraat 50 (CBK Rotterdam). The CBK site describes TENT as one of four CBK programmes, with SIR (Sculpture International Rotterdam), BKOR (public art collection and advice) and Art Office, which offers Rotterdam visual artists support through financial arrangements, meetings and an online community.
CBK Rotterdam was founded in 1982. It was a municipal branch of service until 1 January 2006, when it became an independent foundation with a Supervisory Board (CBK Rotterdam).
The Coolhaven building is a former port laboratory of Dr. Verwey, where food and animal feed were analysed for about seventy years. It was reconstructed for contemporary art exhibitions (museum.nl).

Programme: TENT (IN) and TENT (OUT) exhibitions and projects, events, education, the podcast "Up Close", guest programming and an archive. The current exhibition is "Peel the Power", 18 July to 25 October 2026 (stated by the space).
Visiting: open Thursday to Sunday 12:00 to 18:00 (stated by the space). The Netherlands Museum Pass is valid, and the venue is wheelchair accessible (museum.nl).
details.funding_verdict: TENT: a programme of CBK Rotterdam, a foundation that was a municipal service until 2006
funding: TENT is run by CBK Rotterdam, based at Eendrachtsstraat 10, Rotterdam, which also runs BKOR, which manages the collection of sculptures in Rotterdam's public space and advises the municipality, citizens and artists on public works of art (CBK Rotterdam).
CBK Rotterdam was a municipal branch of service until 1 January 2006 (CBK Rotterdam).
details.bottom_line: TENT is a programme of CBK Rotterdam, which was a municipal branch of service until it became an independent foundation on 1 January 2006, and which also runs BKOR, the manager of Rotterdam's public sculpture collection.

name: Van Schijndel House
funding: Not confirmed. The volunteer-run Mart van Schijndel Foundation (set up 2008) runs visits for a EUR 45 donation. The house is still privately lived in and no owner is named.
watch: Mart van Schijndel designed it for himself and finished it in 1993. Utrecht municipal monument since 1999. Tours by appointment, groups of up to 10.
records_note: Publishes tour terms and donation rates only.
affiliations_note: Tours run by the Mart van Schijndel Foundation, which sells the house's book. Iconic Houses hosts its visiting page and members pay half. Listed in the Iconic Houses network.

overview: House at Pieterskerkhof 8 in the old centre of Utrecht, built on an inner courtyard and largely hidden from the street (Iconic Houses).

The architect Mart van Schijndel (1943 to 1999) bought the former Stichtse Glashandel there in 1988, built the house inside the walls of the old hall in 1992 and finished it in 1993 (DUIC 2016, Iconic Houses).
Named for Van Schijndel, who designed it for himself.

It is built around a triangular hall that serves as the living room, with two patios, glass facades partly of sandblasted glass and doors that hinge on silicone glue. It won the Rietveld Prize in 1995 and became a Utrecht municipal monument in 1999 (Iconic Houses, DUIC 2016).
On site: guided tours, and the Mart van Schijndel Foundation sells the book about the house (Iconic Houses).

Visiting: tours on the first Sunday of each month by appointment, up to 10 people, for a donation of EUR 45 with coffee or tea. Students, Docomomo members, friends of the foundation and Iconic Houses members pay EUR 22.50. Private tours need a donation of at least EUR 350. The pages read say nothing on accessibility.
details.funding_verdict: Van Schijndel House: not confirmed: tour donations through a volunteer-run foundation; no accounts, owner or funder named
funding: Van Schijndel financed the build in 1992 by turning the 1939 gatehouse into four apartments (DUIC 2016).

The Mart van Schijndel Foundation runs the visits and its contact is Natascha Drabbe; Iconic Houses hosts the visiting page (Iconic Houses). Drabbe is an architecture historian and the director and founder of Iconic Houses, and DUIC reports that she lives in the house (Herenhuis 2022, DUIC 2016 and 2024).
details.bottom_line: Nothing verifiable shows who pays for the house: it runs on tour donations through a foundation whose contact is the resident and the head of the network that lists it. Weak points: no named owner and no accounts or board. Worth watching: the ownership of Pieterskerkhof 8 and any change in who opens the house.

name: African Artists' Foundation
watch: Deutsche Bank is listed under 'Sponsors and Partners' on AAF's collaborators page.
why_flagged: Deutsche Bank is listed under 'Sponsors and Partners' on AAF's collaborators page.
records_note: The collaborators page shows undated logos, mostly without alt text. The team page lists staff, not a board.
affiliations_note: Its Collaborators page names SCCA Tamale and Les Ateliers Coffi; LagosPhoto Festival is its own programme.

overview: Non-profit art organisation at 3B Isiola Oyekan Close, off Adeleke Adedoyin Street, Victoria Island, Lagos.
Founded in 2007 by Azu Nwagbogu (Wikipedia).

Runs the LagosPhoto festival, founded in 2009, and ran the National Art Competition, founded in 2008. The site lists a Magnum Photos collaboration, "Beyond the Silence", and "Dig Where You Stand" among past shows.
In October 2020 AAF was evicted from the building it rented from the Umanah family, after Keystone Bank claimed the family's properties through a court order (ThisDay).
The eviction halted most activity for about two years and put the 2021 LagosPhoto on hold. The board then decided to move to another African country, which ThisDay did not name.
Open Tuesday to Friday 10:00 to 18:00 and Saturday 11:00 to 18:00 (stated by the space).
details.funding_verdict: African Artists' Foundation: mixed: private foundations, foreign cultural bodies and corporate sponsors
funding: Nigerian Breweries Plc and AAF jointly announced the 2016 National Art Competition; the prizes were 2 million naira for the grand winner and 1 million naira for each of two other awards (Nigerian Breweries).

AAF's undated "Sponsors and Partners" logos include the Ford Foundation, Open Society Foundations, Mondriaan Fonds, Outset, Goethe-Institut, Alliance Française, the Spanish Embassy, Canon, National Geographic, Vontobel, Nigerian Breweries and Deutsche Bank (stated by the space; only the Goethe-Institut logo has alt text, the other names are read from image file names).

red_flags.heading: Deutsche Bank on the sponsor list
points: A Deutsche Bank logo appears under "Sponsors and Partners" on AAF's collaborators page, with no date and no alt text; the name is read from the image file name.

press.overall: Little criticism. The only critique on record concerns LagosPhoto showing too few Nigerian artists, and Nwagbogu answered it.

items.title: Joe Penney, "LagosPhoto is Five Years Old" (2014)
points: Records the complaint that LagosPhoto does not show enough Nigerians and that some see AAF as elitist.
Nwagbogu answers that few Nigerians apply and that "we will not show your work just because we have an obligation to show Nigerians."

items.title: Yinka Olatunbosun, "On Chokehold, LagosPhoto Festival Looks Elsewhere" (year not stated on the page)
points: Not criticism of AAF: reports the Keystone Bank eviction, AAF's claim of 600 million naira under an indemnity clause, and the bank's reply that the Umanah family, not the bank, caused the closure.

details.bottom_line: The money is a mix of private foundations, European cultural agencies and a few corporate sponsors, none with published amounts. The weak points are the undated Deutsche Bank listing and the lack of any accounts or board list. The tobacco flag on the record is not supported by any source found.

name: April 25 Film Studio
funding: State studio of the Korean People's Army, paid from the state budget. It makes military-themed films about the army, navy, air force and special forces (Koryo Tours).
watch: Founded in 1959 as the February 8 Cinema Studio. Not usually open to visitors, though tour groups have watched films in its cinema.
why_flagged: State studio of the Korean People's Army, paid from the state budget. It makes military-themed films about the army, navy, air force and special forces (Koryo Tours).
affiliations_note: Run by the Korean People's Army (Wikipedia). One of North Korea's state film studios, beside the Korean Art Film Studio, the Korean Documentary Film Studio and SEK Studio.

overview: Film studio of the Korean People's Army at the southern edge of urban Pyongyang, just before the Monument to the Three Charters of National Reunification (Koryo Tours).
Wikipedia dates its founding to 1959 under the name February 8 Cinema Studio. Koryo Tours says the site was built in the early 1960s.
Named for 25 April, which North Korea marks as the army's foundation day. The date marked earlier was 8 February (Koryo Tours).
Koryo Tours calls them propaganda films and names Order 027 and Wolmido as examples.
The main building has a large mosaic of soldiers on its front and a thousand-seat cinema (Koryo Tours).
Koryo Tours says the complex is not usually open to visitors, though some tour groups have watched a film in the cinema.
details.funding_verdict: April 25 Film Studio (Pyongyang): state-run: the Korean People's Army's own film studio, part of the North Korean state
funding: Wikipedia lists it as the April 25 Film Studio of the Korean People's Army, one of several state film studios.

The state announces its budget only as yearly percentage changes. KCNA claimed on 24 March 2026 that 2026 revenue would reach 100.5% of 2025 and spending 105.8%, with 15.8% of spending going to national defence.

red_flags.heading: Sanctions, a studio of a sanctioned state body
points: Executive Order 13722 of 15 March 2016 blocks property of the Government of North Korea and the Workers' Party of Korea that is in the United States or in the control of US persons (Federal Register, 18 March 2016). The order does not name the studio.

OFAC added the Korean People's Army, to which the studio belongs, to its sanctions list on 1 June 2017, in the same action as the Ministry of People's Armed Forces (OFAC). The notice names the army, not the studio.

not_related: Wikipedia lists them as separate state film studios beside this one.
details.bottom_line: The studio's money is the North Korean state's, through the army. The Sanctions basis is the weak point: the Government of North Korea is blocked under Executive Order 13722, and OFAC listed the army itself in 2017.

sources.note: copy of a KCNA text; state media

name: April 25 House of Culture
funding: Military venue opened on 7 October 1975 for military education; its April 25 Culture and Art Composition Office organizes the army's major cultural events.
watch: Hosted the Workers' Party's 6th to 9th congresses. Both the Government of North Korea and the Workers' Party are blocked under US Executive Order 13722.
why_flagged: Military venue opened on 7 October 1975 for military education; its April 25 Culture and Art Composition Office organizes the army's major cultural events.
affiliations_note: Home of the April 25 Culture and Art Composition Office; stage of the Korean People's Army Ensemble and the Moranbong Band, per Koryo Tours.

overview: Theatre and culture venue on Pipha Street in Moranbong District, Pyongyang, near the Metro Museum and the Chinese Embassy (Wikipedia; Koryo Tours).
Opened on 7 October 1975 as the February 8 House of Culture, a venue for military education. Renamed April 25 later (Koryo Tours; Wikipedia).
Named for 25 April, the date North Korea gives for the founding of the anti-Japanese guerrilla army that the Korean People's Army treats as its predecessor (Koryo Tours).
A colonnaded building 105 metres wide, 176 metres deep and almost 50 metres high, with theatres of 6,000 and 1,100 seats, a 600-seat cinema and about 600 other rooms (Koryo Tours; Wikipedia).

Home to the April 25 Culture and Art Composition Office, which organises the army's major cultural events, and a stage for the Korean People's Army Ensemble and the Moranbong Band (Koryo Tours; Wikipedia).

Koryo Tours says it is not generally open to tourists, mainly because it is a military site, though tourists could attend the closing ceremony of the 2006 Pyongyang International Film Festival held there.
details.funding_verdict: April 25 House of Culture (Pyongyang): state-run: a military and party venue of the North Korean state
funding: Koryo Tours calls the house a military site, and says it was built for military education.

The state announces its budget only as yearly percentage changes. KCNA claimed on 24 March 2026 that 2026 revenue would reach 100.5% of 2025 and spending 105.8%, with funds for the cultural sector at 103.1% of last year's and 15.8% of spending going to national defence.

red_flags.heading: Sanctions, a venue of the party and the army
points: Executive Order 13722 of 15 March 2016 blocks property of the Government of North Korea and the Workers' Party of Korea that is in the United States or in the control of US persons (Federal Register, 18 March 2016). The order does not name the house.
The Workers' Party held its congresses here: the 6th in October 1980, the 7th in 2016, the 8th in January 2021 and the 9th on 19 to 25 February 2026 (Wikipedia).

The house was built for military education, and its resident office organises the army's events (Koryo Tours). OFAC added the Korean People's Army to its sanctions list on 1 June 2017 (OFAC); the notice names the army, not the house.

not_related: the April 25 Film Studio, a separate studio of the Korean People's Army (Koryo Tours; Wikipedia).

press.overall: Two news reports citing anonymous sources describe incidents at the building: a fire in 2014 and graffiti in 2018.

items.title: Kim Jun-ho, "Big fire breaks out at Pyongyang's April 25 House of Culture" (2014; byline romanised and title translated from Korean)
points: Unverified: Radio Free Asia reported on 25 April 2014, citing an anonymous Pyongyang resident who had visited China, that a fire started in the building's ceiling a few days earlier; the resident declined to give details of the damage.
The resident said Pyongyang rumours blamed a South Korean intelligence agent.
Radio Free Asia says the army anniversary meetings of 2012 and 2013 were held at the house, while the 24 April 2014 meeting was held at the People's Palace of Culture.

items.title: Lee Sang Yong, "Graffiti directly criticising Kim Jong Un found at Pyongyang's April 25 House of Culture" (2018; byline romanised and title translated from Korean)
points: Unverified: Daily NK reported on 19 March 2018, citing an anonymous Pyongyang source, that graffiti directly criticising Kim Jong Un was found on the side of the building at about 4 a.m. on 1 March.
The source told Daily NK that the authorities tightened checks on people moving about and began handwriting investigations.
Notes that the party congress was held at the house in 2016, the first in 36 years.

details.bottom_line: The money behind the house is the North Korean state's, through the army and the party. The Sanctions basis is the weak point: the Government and the Party are both blocked under Executive Order 13722, the Party has held four congresses here, and OFAC listed the army in 2017. Worth watching: use of the house for state ceremonies and the army's events.

sources.note: copy of a KCNA text; state media

name: Foreign Languages Publishing House
funding: State publisher under the Workers' Party of Korea's Propaganda and Agitation Department, paid from party and state budgets. It publishes the Pyongyang Times and Korea Today for foreign readers.
watch: KCNA marked its 50th anniversary on 4 December 1999. It is on no sanctions list; the flag rests on control by the blocked Workers' Party.
why_flagged: State publisher under the Workers' Party of Korea's Propaganda and Agitation Department, paid from party and state budgets. It publishes the Pyongyang Times and Korea Today for foreign readers.
records_note: The publisher posts the Pyongyang Times and other titles online but no accounts.
affiliations_note: Reports to the Propaganda and Agitation Department of the Workers' Party of Korea. KCNA listed its units in 1999: publishing houses for the Pyongyang Times, Korea Today and other titles, a printing plant and a school for translators. It runs the Naenara and Publications of the DPRK portals (Wikipedia).

overview: State publisher of foreign-language material. A 1999 KCNA item places the press group in the Sosong district of Pyongyang, and Wikipedia's Korea Today page gives Sochong-dong, Sosong District. Wikipedia's page on the house says Potonggang district and cites a link that is now dead.

KCNA reported on 10 December 1999 that the press group marked the 50th anniversary of its establishment on 4 December, which puts the founding in 1949, and said it began by publishing a magazine called New Korea. Wikipedia gives the founding as 10 December 1949 and cites that same KCNA item, whose dateline is 10 December.
Publishes the Pyongyang Times, Korea Today, Korea and Foreign Trade of the DPRK, and runs the Naenara and Publications of the DPRK web portals (Wikipedia).

KCNA's 1999 item lists its units: publishing houses for the pictorial Korea, the Pyongyang Times, foreign-language magazines, foreign trade, Korea Today and information services, a foreign-language printing plant and a school for training translators.
KCNA claimed its periodicals reached at least 160 countries and international organisations.
Wikipedia says it employs a small group of foreigners to revise translations.
details.funding_verdict: Foreign Languages Publishing House: party-controlled: the Workers' Party of Korea's Propaganda and Agitation Department, plus the state
funding: The house is under the control of the Propaganda and Agitation Department of the Workers' Party of Korea, which also decides on its staff (Wikipedia).

North Korea announces its state budget as yearly percentage changes, not amounts. KCNA claimed on 24 March 2026 that 2026 revenue would reach 100.5 percent of 2025 and spending 105.8 percent, with funds for the cultural sector at 103.1 percent of last year's and 15.8 percent of spending going to national defence.

red_flags.heading: Sanctions, house controlled by the Workers' Party
points: Basis: Executive Order 13722 (15 March 2016) blocks the property of the Government of North Korea and of the Workers' Party of Korea (Federal Register).
The house reports to the party's Propaganda and Agitation Department (Wikipedia).

not_related: the Foreign Languages Publishing Houses of Moscow and Hanoi (now Thế Giới Publishers) and Foreign Languages Press, Beijing. Wikipedia lists them as similar publishers in the Soviet Union, Vietnam and China, which makes them separate organisations in other countries.
details.bottom_line: The house is controlled by the Workers' Party and backed by the state, and Executive Order 13722 blocks both. The reporting line to the party's Propaganda and Agitation Department is the point to watch.
